title: Virtual memory
starter: You open ten browser tabs, a game and a video editor on an old laptop. Describe what happens and why.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: When RAM runs out
facts: Every open program needs space in RAM.
When RAM is full, something has to move out to make room.
Without virtual memory, the computer would refuse to open anything else.
stations.challenge: What happens if you open a graphics app when RAM is already full?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Every open program needs space in RAM.
Also credit: When RAM is full, something has to move out to make room.

questions.q: What happens when RAM becomes full?
questions.a: Data that isn't being used right now is moved to secondary storage to free up space

questions.q: Which is most likely to fill RAM?
questions.a: Having many large programs open at once

stations.name: What is virtual memory?
facts: A section of secondary storage used as if it were extra RAM.
Data not currently needed is moved there, freeing RAM for what is needed.
The CPU can only work with data in RAM, so anything needed must be moved back first.
stations.challenge: Write a definition of virtual memory.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A section of secondary storage used as if it were extra RAM.
Also credit: Data not currently needed is moved there, freeing RAM for what is needed.

questions.a: Space on secondary storage used as extra RAM when RAM is full

questions.q: Can the CPU work directly on data held in virtual memory?
questions.a: No: it must be copied back into RAM first

stations.name: Swapping
facts: Data moves out of RAM to disk, and back again when needed: this is swapping, or paging.
If the CPU needs something that isn't in RAM, something else must move out to make room.
Every swap takes time, because secondary storage is slow.
stations.challenge: Explain what happens when a program in virtual memory is needed again.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Data moves out of RAM to disk, and back again when needed: this is swapping, or paging.
Also credit: If the CPU needs something that isn't in RAM, something else must move out to make room.

questions.q: Put the steps in order for when the CPU needs data that is in virtual memory.
questions.a: The CPU asks for data that isn't in RAM → Something not currently needed is moved from RAM to the disk → The data is copied from the disk into the free space in RAM → The CPU can now use the data

stations.name: Why it's slow
facts: Secondary storage is thousands of times slower than RAM.
Heavy swapping is sometimes called disk thrashing: the computer spends more time swapping than working.
You notice it as constant disk activity and everything feeling sluggish.
stations.challenge: Why does a computer relying on virtual memory feel so slow?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Secondary storage is thousands of times slower than RAM.
Also credit: Heavy swapping is sometimes called disk thrashing: the computer spends more time swapping than working.

questions.q: Why is virtual memory slower than RAM?
questions.a: Secondary storage takes far longer to read and write than RAM
The computer spending most of its time swapping data instead of doing useful work

stations.name: Avoiding virtual memory
facts: Install more RAM so more can stay in memory.
An SSD makes swapping less painful, but it's still far slower than RAM.
stations.challenge: Why does doubling the RAM make a computer significantly faster?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Install more RAM so more can stay in memory.
Also credit: Close programs you aren't using.

questions.q: What is the best way to avoid heavy use of virtual memory?
Why does doubling RAM make a heavily loaded computer much faster?
questions.a: Far less swapping is needed, so the CPU waits for the disk much less often

stations.name: Virtual memory in action
facts: A user has a word processor and a browser open, filling RAM.
They open a graphics app, so the least-used data is swapped out to disk.
Switching back to the word processor swaps it in again, which is why the switch feels slow.
stations.challenge: Illustrate this scenario on your worksheet.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A user has a word processor and a browser open, filling RAM.
Also credit: They open a graphics app, so the least-used data is swapped out to disk.

questions.q: The user switches back to the swapped-out word processor. What happens?
questions.a: It is copied back into RAM, and something else is swapped out

questions.q: Which would remove the delay completely?
questions.a: Having enough RAM to hold all three programs at once

final.name: Final challenge: the swap

questions.q: Is each statement about virtual memory true or false?
questions.a: It uses secondary storage as extra memory = True; The CPU can work on it directly, without using RAM = False; It is slower than using RAM = True; It is needed because RAM is limited = True; Adding more RAM reduces how much it is used = True; It makes a computer faster than having enough RAM = False

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by virtual memory.
points: Without virtual memory, the computer would refuse to open anything else.
Install more RAM so more can stay in memory.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: Explain why using virtual memory slows a computer down.
points: Without virtual memory, the computer would refuse to open anything else.
Heavy swapping is sometimes called disk thrashing: the computer spends more time swapping than working.
Install more RAM so more can stay in memory.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: State one way a user could reduce the need for virtual memory.
points: Without virtual memory, the computer would refuse to open anything else.
Install more RAM so more can stay in memory.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark for a correct answer.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
